content: Shea butter, also known as shea nut butter, is a natural fat that is slightly yellowish or ivory in color. It is derived from the fruit of the shea tree through a process of crushing and boiling. This substance is widely utilized in the cosmetics industry as both a moisturizer and an emollient. Additionally, shea butter is edible and is used as a cooking oil in West Africa. It is also occasionally employed in the chocolate industry as a substitute for cocoa butter. The shea tree, scientifically named Vitellaria paradoxa (formerly Butyrospermum parkii), begins to bear fruit resembling large plums at approximately 20 years of age. It reaches full fruit production around the age of 45 and can continue producing nuts for up to 200 years after reaching maturity. The tree is known by various vernacular names across its extensive range, which spans nearly 5,000 kilometers from Senegal in the west to Uganda in the east across the African continent. The nomenclature of the shea tree has undergone a complex evolution since the first recorded specimen was collected by Scottish explorer Mungo Park on May 26, 1797. The tree is now classified under the genus Vitellaria, with subspecies paradoxa and nilotica. It typically grows to an average height of about 15 meters, with abundant branches and thick, waxy, deeply fissured bark that provides fire resistance. The shea tree grows naturally in the wild, predominantly in the dry savannah belt of West Africa, extending from Senegal in the west to Sudan in the east, and reaching the foothills of the Ethiopian highlands. It is found in 19 African countries, including Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Ethiopia, Ghana, Guinea Bissau, Côte d'Ivoire, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Sudan, Togo, Uganda, Zaire, and Guinea. In Ghana, the tree is particularly abundant in the Guinea savannah and less so in the Sudan savannah. It covers nearly the entire area of Northern Ghana, spanning approximately 77,670 square kilometers, with the densest stands found in Eastern Gonja. Sparse shea tree coverage is also observed in the Brong-Ahafo, Ashanti, Eastern, and Volta regions in the southern part of the country. Shea butter is renowned for its cosmetic properties, particularly as a moisturizer and emollient. It also exhibits anti-inflammatory properties. It is marketed as being effective in treating a variety of skin conditions, including fading scars, eczema, burns, rashes, acne, severely dry skin, blemishes, dark spots, skin discolorations, chapped lips, stretch marks, wrinkles, and reducing the irritation associated with psoriasis. Shea butter provides natural ultraviolet (UV) sun protection, although the level of protection is highly variable, ranging from none to approximately SPF 6. Individuals with sun sensitivity should not rely on shea butter for adequate sun protection. It absorbs rapidly into the skin without leaving a greasy residue. Compared to other emollients, shea butter is richer, but its limited supply leads to fluctuating market prices. Shea butter is a common ingredient in many high-end moisturizing skin products due to its skin-softening effects. It is also used in hair conditioners to add and retain moisture in dry, brittle hair, as well as to revitalize and prevent breakage. In some indigenous ceremonies, shea butter holds cultural significance. For example, members of the Holy Spirit Movement rebel group in Uganda applied shea butter to their bodies, believing it would protect them from bullets. In Togo, West Africa, handcrafted shea butter is used in ceremonies among the Fulani ethnic group. Additionally, many artisans who carve djembe shells and other African drum shells use shea butter to condition the wood. It is also applied to condition the goat or cow skin drumheads of these instruments.
